citation.title: Can Large Language Models Transform Computational Social Science?
citation.type: publisher's version (MIT Press, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, accepted 25 October 2023), 55 pages

question: Whether zero-shot large language models can augment or replace human annotation in computational social science: how well they perform, which model to choose, in which domains they are useful, and how they can be used (four research questions).
data: Benchmarks in English from computational social science. The abstract says 25 tasks; one place in the text says 24 (inconsistency in the source). Thirteen models: FLAN-T5 (six sizes), UL2, GPT-3 text-001/002/003, gpt-3.5-turbo and GPT-4. Each task is tested on a class-stratified sample of at most 500 instances from the dataset's test set. Fine-tuned baselines: RoBERTa-large (classification) and T5-base (generation).
method: Zero-shot prompting with the original prompt plus 4 paraphrases (5 prompts), temperature 0. Macro F1 averaged over the 5 prompts for classification and structured parsing; Cohen's kappa against gold labels (Table 4); comparison with fine-tuned baselines; error analysis of shared errors (gold mislabels, plausible secondary labels, over-prediction of neutral categories); few-shot (3 and 5 examples) test; human evaluation for generation tasks (expert Likert scores, author ranking). Also describes Design-based Semi-supervised Learning (DSL) as a way to get unbiased estimates from LLM labels plus a small set of gold labels. Prompt design guidelines in Table 1.

definitions.definition: The development and application of computational methods to the scientific analysis of behavioral and linguistic data.
definitions.quote: the development and application of computational methods to the scientiﬁc analysis of behavioral and linguistic data

findings.claim: On classification tasks LLMs do not beat the best fine-tuned models but reach fair agreement with humans.
findings.quote: On taxonomic labeling tasks (classiﬁcation), LLMs fail to outperform the best ﬁne-tuned models but still achieve fair levels of agreement with humans.

findings.claim: Prompted LLMs do not match fine-tuned classifiers, and the best LLM performance is often too low to replace human annotation.
findings.quote: prompted LLMs do not match or exceed the performance of carefully ﬁne-tuned classiﬁers, and the best LLM performance is often too low to entirely replace human annotation.

findings.claim: Models hedged under uncertainty, refused offensive content and generalised beyond the given labels.
findings.quote: we found that models would hedge in the case of uncertainty, refuse to engage with offensive language, and attempt to generalize beyond provided labels.

findings.claim: Authors recommend human-in-the-loop use (a recommendation, not a measured finding).
findings.quote: we recommend human-in-the-loop methods to mitigate bias and risk

findings.claim: With few gold labels, DSL gives confidence intervals with good coverage.
findings.quote: With only 25 gold annotations, DSL can compute conﬁdence intervals that have >86% correct coverage

findings.claim: Authors argue human validation is needed to avoid a replication crisis from LLM errors (argument).
findings.quote: Human validation is key to avoiding a replication crisis in CSS caused by LLM hallucinations and inaccuracies.

findings.claim: Ensembling does not fix label corruption because LLMs agree with themselves even when wrong.
findings.quote: Ensembling prediction does not mitigate this label corruption as LLMs demonstrate high internal agreement, even when inaccurate

limitations.point: Authors ask for caution in reading the results.
limitations.quote: We urge readers to interpret the results with caution

limitations.point: LLMs may lack representations for technical terms (domain-specific label sets).
limitations.quote: may lack sufﬁcient representations for such technical terms

limitations.point: Possible training-data leakage can inflate test performance.
No systematic analysis of bias and performance differences across groups (quote not re-verified; see pages_read).
limitations.quote: we were unable to perform a systematic analysis of biases and performance discrepancies

limitations.point: Tested on English benchmarks of social-media, news and similar text; no test on organisation names, delegate lists or business sectors (this is a gap in the source, not stated by the authors).
